name: Persimmon

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Persimmon is easygoing about soil but wants one thing above all: good drainage. A deep, well-drained loam is ideal, and a sandy loam or lighter sandy soil works fine too. The trouble spot is heavy clay that holds water, because persimmon roots, especially on Asian types, are prone to root rot in soggy ground. If your soil is heavy or wet, plant on a raised mound so the roots sit above standing water. A soil of ordinary richness suits it; persimmon needs little feeding and too much can cause the fruit to drop.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Persimmon is broadly soil-tolerant but demands good drainage, ideally a deep, well-drained loam; a sandy loam is well suited and lighter sandy soils are workable. Heavy, water-holding clay is the problem texture, since persimmon (especially Diospyros kaki) is susceptible to root and crown rot on poorly drained sites; on such ground plant on a raised berm. Best sites are upland sandy loams. Moderate fertility is plenty, and persimmon is sensitive to salinity and to excess nitrogen, which triggers fruit drop.

ph.note_beginner: Persimmon does best in a slightly acidic soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and is fine up to about 7.0 (pH is just a measure of how acidic or alkaline the soil is). Test your soil before planting the permanent tree. If it is too acidic, garden lime raises the pH; if it is too alkaline, elemental sulfur lowers it. Mix any amendment in before planting, since pH changes slowly and is far easier to correct before the tree is in the ground.
ph.note_seasoned: Persimmon prefers a slightly acidic pH 6.0 to 6.5 and tolerates up to about 7.0. Test before planting and adjust gradually: lime raises a too-acidic pH, elemental sulfur lowers one that is too alkaline. Work amendments in ahead of planting the permanent tree, since pH shifts slowly and is easiest to correct before establishment.

fertilizer.timing: late dormancy, split with early and late summer
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Persimmon needs little feeding and is easily over-fed: excess nitrogen causes premature fruit drop. A light program suits it, split across the season on sandy soils (the bulk in late dormancy, a lighter touch in early and late summer), broadcast evenly around the root zone to the drip line and kept off the trunk. On decent soil an established tree may need no fertilizer at all; feed only if growth is weak or leaves are pale.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Persimmon barely needs feeding, and too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, makes the fruit drop off. Go light. Scatter it evenly on the soil around the tree out to where the branches reach, keep it off the trunk, and water it in. On good soil an older tree may need nothing at all, so only feed if the tree looks weak or the leaves are pale.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 is plenty for persimmon; the tree is a light feeder and over-fertilizing, particularly with nitrogen, drops fruit rather than improving it. Err toward less.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: A balanced fertilizer like 10-10-10 (the three numbers are nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium) is all persimmon needs, and often it needs none. Do not overdo it, because too much, especially the first number, nitrogen, makes the fruit fall off.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: A common home rate is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 per year of tree age, applied in late dormancy (roughly March), with lighter follow-up feedings in early and late summer where the soil is sandy. Cap it at a modest total for a mature tree and do not fertilize at planting. If growth is already vigorous, skip feeding entirely; excess nitrogen shows up as dropped fruit, not bigger crops.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: A simple rule is about 2 ounces of 10-10-10 for each year of the tree's age, given in late winter, with a little more in early and late summer if your soil is sandy. Do not feed a tree that is already growing well, and never put fertilizer in the planting hole. If in doubt, feed less: too much makes persimmons drop.

companions.note_beginner: Most Asian persimmons are self-fruitful, so one tree fruits on its own and you do not need a partner tree. American persimmons are different: they usually have male and female trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon nearby to fruit, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. For a tree, the pairings that matter are not vegetable-garden companions but what grows around the roots: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under the branches, since lawn competes with a young tree, and a mulched, weed-free circle helps it settle in. Persimmon is a low-pest, easygoing tree, so there is little else to fuss over.
companions.note_seasoned: Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is self-fruitful, so a single tree crops without a pollinizer; American persimmon (D. virginiana) is typically dioecious and a female needs a male within roughly 50 to 200 feet, the exception being self-fruitful selections like Meader. The interactions that matter for a tree concern the root zone, not classic vegetable companions: keep turf and weeds cleared back from under the canopy, since grass competes hard with a young tree, and a mulched, competition-free root area speeds establishment. Persimmon is notably low-pest and low-maintenance, so companion planting is a minor consideration here.

good_seasoned.name: Flowering herbs and pollinator plants
good_seasoned.label: traditional

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Orchard-floor insectary logic is sound and extension-aligned in principle: flowering plants recruit the natural enemies (parasitic wasps, ladybugs, hoverflies) that hold persimmon's soft-bodied pests (scale, mealybug, psyllid) in check, and UC IPM's persimmon guidance leans on preserving natural enemies. But persimmon is self-fruitful/parthenocarpic, so the pollinator draw is not needed for fruit set, and the predator-recruitment benefit is diffuse and unquantified for persimmon specifically. traditional/medium.

good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A skirt of flowering herbs and pollinator plants around a persimmon supports orchard-floor health. Because persimmon is self-fruitful and its Asian cultivars set fruit parthenocarpically, the pollinator draw is a bonus rather than a requirement, but the same flowers recruit the ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps that keep scale, mealybug, and persimmon psyllid at tolerable levels, which is exactly the natural-enemy approach UC IPM recommends for this low-spray tree. Keep the plantings out toward the drip line rather than crowding the trunk.

bad_seasoned.name: Lawn and weeds crowding the young trunk
bad_seasoned.label: research_backed

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Keeping turf and weeds cleared from a young fruit tree's root zone is standard, well-evidenced extension practice: grass competes strongly with a young tree for water and nitrogen and slows establishment, and a mulched weed-free circle is the routine recommendation across fruit-tree extension guidance. extension_backed/high for the general fruit-tree principle applied to persimmon.

bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Grass and weeds pressed up against a young persimmon are the pairing to avoid. Turf competes hard with a newly planted tree for water and nitrogen and measurably slows establishment, and growth against the trunk also traps moisture and invites string-trimmer wounds. Keep a mulched, weed-free circle a few feet out from the trunk through the establishment years, keeping the mulch itself off the bark.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small, immobile bumps on bark, twigs, and the underside of leaves; white peach scale shows as snow-white encrustations on the trunk and limbs, while soft scales are brown and rounded. Heavy infestations produce sticky honeydew that blackens with sooty mold and draws ants. Vigor and fruit quality decline where scale builds up unchecked.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Little bumps stuck to the bark, twigs, and leaf undersides that do not move. White peach scale looks like snow-white crust on the trunk and branches; other scales are small brown domes. They leave a sticky coating (honeydew) that turns black with sooty mold and attracts ants. Bad cases slowly weaken the tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several scale species, notably white peach scale and soft scales (Parthenolecanium spp.), which insert their mouthparts and feed on sap under a protective waxy shell. Their honeydew supports sooty mold. Populations flare where natural enemies have been knocked back by broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.cause_beginner: Tiny sap-sucking insects that hide under a waxy shell, mainly white peach scale and soft scales. They feed on the tree's sap and drip sticky honeydew that grows black mold. They get worse when sprays kill off the helpful insects that normally eat them.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Preserve natural enemies (ladybugs, parasitic wasps) by not spraying broadly, since they usually hold scale to tolerable levels on persimmon. Prune out and destroy heavily encrusted wood. A dormant-season horticultural oil application smothers overwintering scale on the bark and is the main direct control for a backyard tree.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let the helpful bugs do the work by avoiding broad sprays, since ladybugs and tiny wasps usually keep scale in check on persimmon. Cut out and throw away badly crusted branches. A spray of horticultural oil while the tree is leafless in winter smothers the scale on the bark and is the simplest hands-on control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep the tree vigorous, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt biological control, and monitor the trunk and scaffolds for early white encrustations so a dormant oil can be timed before populations explode.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree healthy, skip the broad bug sprays that kill the good insects, and check the trunk and branches now and then for the first white crusty patches so you can put on a winter oil spray before it spreads.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, oval insects coated in white, cottony wax clustered in leaf axils, under the calyx of the fruit, and along shoots. Like scale, they excrete honeydew that fosters sooty mold and ants, and feeding under the calyx can contaminate and blemish fruit.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small soft insects covered in white, cottony fluff, tucked into leaf joints, under the leafy cap of the fruit, and along stems. They leave the same sticky honeydew and black mold as scale, and where they hide under the fruit's cap they can spoil its look.
pests.cause_seasoned: Mealybugs (several species) that suck phloem sap and shelter in protected crevices, including beneath the fruit calyx. Ant-tended colonies persist because ants protect them from natural enemies for the honeydew.
pests.cause_beginner: Sap-sucking insects called mealybugs that hide in sheltered spots, including under the leafy cap on the fruit. Ants often protect them because they want the sweet honeydew, which lets the mealybugs build up.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rely first on natural enemies, which generally keep mealybugs below damaging levels on landscape fruit trees; avoid the broad-spectrum sprays that disrupt them. Control honeydew-farming ants (sticky trunk bands) so predators can work. Spot-treat visible colonies with a horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Let natural predators handle most mealybugs, and avoid broad sprays that kill those helpers. Stop ants from climbing the trunk with a sticky band so the predators can reach the mealybugs. Dab visible clusters with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain biological control by minimizing broad-spectrum sprays, manage ants, and inspect the calyx end of developing fruit where mealybugs hide, removing infested fruit early.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep the helpful insects around by not spraying broadly, keep ants off the tree, and check under the cap of the growing fruit where mealybugs like to hide, picking off any infested ones early.

pests.name: Persimmon psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: New leaves curl, roll, and cup around the feeding of tiny nymphs in spring, often distorting the flush of young growth. Small crawlers and their waxy filaments may be visible inside the rolled leaves. Damage is largely cosmetic on an established tree but can stunt young shoots.
pests.symptoms_beginner: In spring the new leaves curl and roll up around tiny insects feeding inside. You may see small crawlers and white waxy threads inside the rolled leaves. On an older tree the harm is mostly cosmetic, but it can slow down a young one.
pests.cause_seasoned: The persimmon psyllid, a small sap-feeding insect whose nymphs feed on expanding leaves in spring and induce the characteristic leaf roll. It is a minor, mostly cosmetic pest of both native and Oriental persimmon.
pests.cause_beginner: A small sap-feeding insect called the persimmon psyllid. Its young feed on the new spring leaves and make them curl. It is a minor pest that mostly just looks bad.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Usually no treatment is warranted; natural enemies and the tree's vigor absorb the damage. On a small tree, prune off and destroy the worst rolled tips in spring. Preserve beneficial insects by avoiding broad sprays.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Usually nothing needs to be done, since the tree shrugs it off. On a small tree you can clip off the worst curled tips in spring. Avoid broad sprays so the helpful insects stay around.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Little is required. Keeping the tree healthy and preserving natural enemies keeps the psyllid a cosmetic nuisance rather than a problem.
pests.prevention_beginner: There is not much to do. A healthy tree with its natural predators intact keeps this pest to a harmless nuisance.

pests.name: Persimmon borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Wilting or dying shoots and, on the trunk, gummy ooze mixed with sawdust-like frass near the base where larvae tunnel the inner bark. Young trees can be girdled and killed; it is the one persimmon pest extension warns can be serious, particularly in the Southeast.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Shoots that wilt or die, and near the bottom of the trunk a sticky ooze mixed with what looks like sawdust, where the larvae are tunneling under the bark. A young tree can be ringed and killed, so this is the one persimmon pest to take seriously.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of the persimmon (and flatheaded) borers that bore into the lower trunk and inner bark. Trees stressed by wounds or drought are attacked first, but healthy bark can also be entered; it affects both native and Oriental persimmon.
pests.cause_beginner: The larvae (grub stage) of borer beetles and moths that tunnel into the lower trunk. Wounded or stressed trees are hit hardest, but a healthy tree can be attacked too.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No spray reaches larvae already inside the trunk. Expose the crown, locate entry holes by the gum and frass, and kill larvae by hand with a wire. Keep the trunk base free of mechanical wounds and remove badly infested young wood.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the larvae are inside, no spray reaches them. Scrape soil away from the base, find the holes marked by gum and sawdust, and kill the grubs with a stiff wire. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk so you are not giving the borers wounds to enter.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Protect the lower trunk from injury, keep the tree vigorous and well watered, and inspect the trunk base each late summer for fresh gum and frass so an infestation is caught in its first year.
pests.prevention_beginner: Keep mowers and string trimmers off the trunk, keep the tree healthy and watered, and check the base of the trunk each late summer for fresh ooze and sawdust so you catch borers early.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken lesions on fruit, and spots and dieback on leaves and young shoots, most damaging in warm, wet weather and humid regions. Infected fruit can rot before or after harvest, and severe leaf infection thins the canopy.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Dark, sunken spots on the fruit and spots or dieback on leaves and new shoots, worst in warm, rainy weather. Bad cases rot the fruit and thin out the leaves.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Anthracnose fungi (Colletotrichum and related genera) that overwinter in dead wood and mummified fruit and spread by rain-splash in warm, humid conditions. Pressure is highest in the wet Southeast and lowest in dry-summer climates.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus (anthracnose) that survives winter in dead wood and old fruit and spreads in warm, wet weather. It is a bigger problem in humid, rainy areas than in dry ones.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sanitation is the core control: prune out and destroy dead and cankered wood and remove mummified fruit, and keep the canopy open so it dries quickly after rain. Remove and dispose of infected fruit promptly. Fungicides are rarely needed on a backyard tree if sanitation is kept up.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Cleanup is the main fix: cut out dead branches, pick off and throw away any shriveled old fruit, and prune so the tree is open and dries fast after rain. Remove spotted fruit as you see it. A home tree rarely needs spraying if you keep it clean.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose an open canopy through pruning, clear fallen and mummified fruit each season, and site the tree with good air movement. In high-pressure humid regions, favor cultivars with better tolerance.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Keep the tree open with light pruning, clean up fallen and dried-up fruit every year, and plant it where air moves freely. In rainy areas, pick a variety known to hold up better.

diseases.name: Root and crown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: General decline, sparse yellowing foliage, and dieback on a tree in heavy or poorly drained soil, with dark, decayed bark and roots at and below the soil line. Asian persimmon is especially susceptible; the tree may collapse over a season or two once the crown is girdled.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: A tree that slowly goes downhill, with thin yellow leaves and dying branches, usually in wet or heavy soil. The bark and roots at the base turn dark and rotten. Asian persimmon is especially prone, and a badly affected tree can die within a year or two.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Soilborne Phytophthora (and related) fungi that attack roots and the crown in waterlogged soil. Oriental persimmon is notably susceptible to root rot, which is a chief reason it is often grafted onto the more tolerant native (D. virginiana) rootstock.
diseases.cause_beginner: Water-mold fungi in the soil (Phytophthora) that rot the roots and crown when the ground stays wet. Asian persimmon is easily hit, which is why it is often grafted onto the tougher native persimmon roots.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once the crown is rotting. Management is prevention through drainage: never plant in standing-water sites, plant on a mound in heavy soil, and choose a tree on tolerant native rootstock where drainage is marginal. Avoid overwatering an established tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Once the base is rotting there is no fixing it, so this one is all about prevention. Never plant where water stands, plant on a raised mound in heavy soil, and pick a tree grafted onto native persimmon roots if your drainage is iffy. Do not overwater an older tree.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant only on well-drained ground or a raised berm, select tolerant (native) rootstock in marginal soils, and water deeply but infrequently rather than keeping the root zone saturated.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Plant only where water drains well, or on a raised mound, choose a tree on native persimmon rootstock if your soil is heavy, and water deeply now and then instead of keeping the soil soggy.

diseases.name: Leaf spot and twig dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Circular to angular leaf spots that may yellow and drop leaves in a wet season, and dieback of small twigs. Usually a minor, cosmetic issue on an otherwise healthy persimmon, which extension sources note has few serious disease problems.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: Round or angular spots on the leaves that can turn them yellow and drop in a wet year, plus a little dieback of small twigs. On a healthy persimmon this is usually minor and just cosmetic.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Several leaf-spot fungi favored by prolonged leaf wetness. Persimmon is generally regarded as having no serious insect or disease problems, so leaf spot is typically a low-impact, weather-driven nuisance.
diseases.cause_beginner: Common leaf-spot fungi that show up when leaves stay wet a long time. Persimmon has few real disease problems, so this is usually just a minor, weather-related annoyance.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen infected leaves to reduce carryover, keep the canopy open, and keep the tree vigorous; fungicides are seldom justified on a home tree.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Rake up and remove fallen spotted leaves, keep the tree open, and keep it healthy. A home tree almost never needs a spray for this.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good air movement, an open canopy, and fall leaf cleanup keep leaf spot to a cosmetic level.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Good airflow, light pruning to keep the tree open, and cleaning up fallen leaves in autumn keep this to a harmless level.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently. A young tree wants a deep soak about once or twice a week through its first two seasons; an established tree is fairly drought-tolerant and does well on roughly weekly deep watering in summer heat, less in cool weather and little through winter dormancy. Persimmon prefers infrequent, thorough irrigation over frequent shallow watering, and standing-wet soil invites root rot.
watering.frequency_beginner: Water deeply now and then rather than a little every day. A young tree needs a deep soak about once or twice a week for its first couple of years. An older tree handles dry spells well and is happy with roughly a weekly deep soak in summer, less when it is cool, and almost nothing in winter. Do not keep the soil soggy, since that causes root rot.
watering.amount_seasoned: Soak deeply enough to wet the full root zone rather than just the surface: on the order of 5 gallons per watering for a young tree, and roughly the equivalent of an inch of water per week for a bearing tree through the growing season, more in extreme heat. Deep, thorough soaks drive the deep rooting that carries an established persimmon through dry stretches.
watering.amount_beginner: Each time you water, give a deep soak that reaches down to the roots, not just a splash on top. A young tree wants about 5 gallons per soak; an older, fruiting tree wants about an inch of water a week through the growing season, and more in a heat wave. Deep soaks build deep roots that handle dry spells.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the root zone with drip or a soaker hose out toward the drip line, keeping the trunk base from staying wet. Persimmon tolerates drought better than waterlogging, so the discipline is deep-then-dry, never continuously saturated. Overhead watering that wets the canopy in humid regions can encourage anthracnose and leaf spot.
watering.method_beginner: Water the ground around the roots with a drip line or soaker hose, out to the edge of the branches, and keep the base of the trunk from sitting wet. Persimmon handles dry better than soggy, so let the soil dry a bit between waterings. In humid areas, avoid spraying water over the leaves, which can bring on leaf diseases.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing leaves, wilting that persists in wet soil, and general decline point to waterlogging and possible root or crown rot, to which persimmon (especially Asian types) is prone. Soil that never dries between waterings is the warning; this is far more dangerous to persimmon than underwatering.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: Yellow leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and a tree slowly going downhill mean too much water and the risk of root rot, which persimmon catches easily. Soil that never dries out is your signal to back off. Overwatering hurts persimmon more than underwatering does.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slowed growth, and, most tellingly, premature fruit drop or small, poorly sized fruit when a tree runs dry during fruit development. An established persimmon endures moderate drought but sizes its crop poorly under sustained water stress.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Wilting, dull or curling leaves, slower growth, and, the clearest sign, fruit dropping early or staying small when the tree gets too dry while the fruit is filling out. An older persimmon can take some dryness, but the crop suffers if it goes too dry for too long.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Through establishment, keep the root ball and surrounding soil evenly moist but never waterlogged. Deep soaks of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, adjusted for rain and heat, build the deep root system persimmon relies on later.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the tree is getting established, keep the soil around the roots evenly moist but not soggy. A deep soak of about 5 gallons once or twice a week, more in heat and less after rain, helps it grow the deep roots it needs.

schedule_by_stage.rate: deep soak, ~1 in per week equivalent
schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: During fruit development, keep moisture steady; sudden drought or a wet-dry swing in this window contributes to premature fruit drop and small fruit. Aim for the equivalent of about an inch of water a week, delivered as deep soaks, more in heat.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: While the fruit is sizing up, keep the water steady. Letting the tree swing from dry to wet now can make the fruit drop or stay small. Aim for about an inch of water a week as deep soaks, more when it is hot.

schedule_by_stage.note_seasoned: Once the tree drops its leaves and goes dormant, water need falls sharply; rely mostly on rainfall and water only in prolonged dry spells. Avoid keeping dormant soil saturated, which favors root rot.
schedule_by_stage.note_beginner: After the leaves fall and the tree is resting, it needs very little water. Let rain do most of the work and only water in long dry stretches. Do not keep the soil soaked in winter.

watering.method_note_seasoned: Water deeply and infrequently at the root zone, ideally by drip or soaker, to encourage deep rooting; let the soil dry between waterings, since persimmon tolerates drought far better than waterlogging. Young trees need consistent moisture through their first two seasons; established trees are moderately drought-tolerant but drop fruit and size poorly under sustained stress.
watering.method_note_beginner: Give deep soaks now and then rather than a little every day, and water at the ground with a drip line or soaker hose, letting the soil dry out a bit between waterings. Persimmon handles dry much better than soggy. Young trees need steady moisture for their first couple of years; older trees take dry spells but drop fruit if left too dry too long.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The sensitive windows are the first two establishment seasons and the fruit-development period from set through sizing, when erratic moisture drives fruit drop. Keep moisture steady through fruit fill; an established tree can ease off during dormancy.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The times to be careful are the first couple of years while the tree establishes, and the stretch when the fruit is growing, since uneven watering then makes fruit drop. Keep the water steady while the fruit fills out; the tree needs little in winter.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Non-astringent types (Fuyu) are eaten firm and hold at room temperature for a week or more, softening slowly. Astringent types (Hachiya) must be held at room temperature until they ripen to a jelly-soft, fully translucent stage before eating; rushing them leaves an intensely puckery, tannic mouthfeel. Persimmons continue to ripen after picking, so counter-ripening astringent fruit is normal practice.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Firm-eaten types like Fuyu keep on the counter for a week or more and just slowly soften. Astringent types like Hachiya need to sit out until they turn completely soft and jelly-like before you eat them, or they taste harshly puckery. Persimmons keep ripening after picking, so leaving astringent ones on the counter to soften is exactly right.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Refrigerate firm non-astringent persimmons to hold them for several weeks; they keep notably better than most tree fruit. Refrigerate soft-ripe astringent fruit only once fully ripe and use within a few days. Chilling can be used to speed some astringent types toward ripeness, but eating quality is best judged by full softness.
storage.fridge_beginner: Firm Fuyu-type persimmons keep in the fridge for several weeks, better than most fruit. Put soft, ripe Hachiya-type fruit in the fridge only once it is fully soft, and eat it within a few days.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Persimmons freeze well as pulp. Scoop the soft, ripe flesh of astringent types, or puree non-astringent flesh, add a little lemon juice to limit browning, and freeze in portions. Frozen pulp keeps for several months and is ideal for baking, cookies, and puddings. Whole astringent fruit can also be frozen and thawed, which softens and de-astringes them.
storage.freezer_beginner: Persimmons freeze nicely as pulp. Scoop out the soft ripe flesh, mix in a little lemon juice so it does not brown, and freeze it in portions. It keeps for months and is great for baking. You can also freeze whole astringent persimmons; thawing softens them and takes away the pucker.
storage.notes_seasoned: The single most common persimmon disappointment is biting an astringent Hachiya-type before it is fully soft. Match handling to type: eat non-astringent Fuyu firm, ripen astringent types to jelly-soft first.
storage.notes_beginner: The number one persimmon mistake is eating an astringent kind before it is completely soft, which is harshly puckery. Eat firm types like Fuyu crisp, and let soft types like Hachiya ripen all the way first.

recommended.name: Fuyu (Jiro)
recommended.recommended_note: The standard non-astringent Asian persimmon: flattened, apple-firm fruit eaten crisp with no astringency, self-fruitful and nearly seedless. The best first tree for most home gardens. About 200 chill hours.

recommended.name: Izu
recommended.recommended_note: An early, compact non-astringent Asian persimmon that ripens about three weeks before Fuyu; very low chill (about 100 hours) and a good choice for small yards and the mildest-winter areas.

recommended.name: Hachiya
recommended.recommended_note: The classic large astringent Asian persimmon: acorn-shaped fruit that is mouth-puckering until it ripens to a sweet, jelly-soft pulp, superb for baking and drying. Self-fruitful. About 200 chill hours.

recommended.name: Great Wall
recommended.recommended_note: A cold-hardy astringent Asian persimmon; grafted on native rootstock it tolerates winters toward 0°F, extending Asian persimmon into colder ground than Fuyu or Hachiya.

recommended.name: Meader
recommended.recommended_note: A self-fruitful American persimmon that sets seedless fruit with no male tree, extremely cold-hardy (to about -25°F). The standard one-tree choice for cold-winter gardens where Asian persimmon will not survive.

recommended.name: Prok
recommended.recommended_note: A large-fruited, productive American persimmon for cold zones. Like most American types it is female and crops best with a male American persimmon nearby; very cold-hardy and reliable.

varieties.note_seasoned: Choose first by type and climate. In zones 7 and warmer, an Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is the usual pick: a self-fruitful, non-astringent Fuyu for firm crisp eating, or an astringent Hachiya for soft-ripe fruit and baking. In colder zones (4 to 6), choose an American persimmon (D. virginiana): a self-fruitful Meader for a single tree, or a hardy female such as Prok with a male pollinizer. Match the cultivar's modest chill requirement to your winters, and favor named grafted cultivars over seedlings for known fruit quality and sex.
varieties.note_beginner: Pick first by type and your climate. In zone 7 and warmer, an Asian persimmon is usually best: a self-fruitful, non-astringent Fuyu to eat crisp, or an astringent Hachiya to eat soft. In colder areas (zones 4 to 6), choose an American persimmon: a self-fruitful Meader for a single tree, or a hardy kind like Prok with a male tree nearby. Persimmon needs little winter cold, so most types suit most winters. Buy a named, grafted tree rather than a seedling so you know the fruit and, for American types, the sex.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Hardening off does not apply to persimmon. It is planted as a dormant bare-root or grafted container tree, not raised from a seedling indoors, so there is no tender transplant to acclimate to the outdoors.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: Hardening off (slowly getting an indoor-grown seedling used to being outside) does not apply to persimmon. You plant it as a dormant bare-root tree or a young grafted tree from a pot, not as a seedling started inside, so there is no tender plant to ease outdoors.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant a dormant bare-root tree in late winter to early spring before bud break, or set a grafted container tree in the cooler months. Persimmon resents root disturbance, so handle the taproot gently and plant promptly. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, set the tree at the depth it grew in the nursery with the graft union above the final soil line, backfill with native soil, water in well, and do not fertilize in the planting hole. On heavy soil, plant on a raised mound for drainage.
start_method.notes_beginner: Plant a bare-root tree in late winter or early spring while it is still leafless, or set a young potted grafted tree in the cooler months. Persimmon does not like having its roots disturbed, so handle them gently and plant it right away. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, set the tree at the same depth it grew before with the graft joint above the soil, fill in with the soil you dug out, and water it in well. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. If your soil is heavy, plant on a raised mound so water drains away.

soil_mix.type_beginner: If you grow a dwarf persimmon in a pot, use a chunky, fast-draining mix made for shrubs and trees, not a soft peat-based potting soil that stays soggy. A bark-based mix (composted bark with perlite or pumice for drainage) gives the roots the air they need. Do not use soil dug from the yard in a pot, because it packs down and drains poorly.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Keep it simple and aim for drainage. If the mix holds water, stir in more perlite or pumice, and lay a thin layer of compost on top instead of mixing lots of rich material throughout. Avoid water-holding crystals and heavy peat, since persimmon roots must not stay wet.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: For a container persimmon (a genetic-dwarf or size-controlled tree), use a coarse, fast-draining soilless mix built for woody plants, not a peat-heavy potting soil. A bark-based mix (composted pine bark with perlite or pumice) supplies the air-filled porosity persimmon roots need; the species is root-rot-prone, so the mix must never stay saturated. Skip native garden soil, which compacts under container irrigation.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Keep amendments minimal and drainage-first: add perlite or pumice if the base mix is water-retentive, and top-dress with a thin layer of compost rather than blending heavy organics throughout. Avoid moisture-retentive crystals or large peat fractions, which work against the free-draining root zone persimmon demands.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: A persimmon in a pot dries out much faster than one in the ground. In summer heat, check it daily and water when the top inch or two is dry, until water runs out the bottom, but never let the pot stand in a saucer of water, since wet roots rot. In winter, when the tree is resting, give just enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Frequent watering washes food out of a pot, so feed lightly. A dilute balanced liquid feed every few weeks from spring into midsummer is plenty, then stop by late summer. Remember persimmon is a light feeder and too much nitrogen drops fruit, so err toward less.
container_notes.notes_beginner: Persimmon really wants to grow in the ground, where it becomes a good-sized tree. A pot is a workaround only for a naturally dwarf variety or where you have no space for a full tree. It can be done, but expect more hands-on watering and smaller crops. Use the biggest well-draining pot you can, and give it winter protection in cold areas.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Persimmon is fundamentally a ground tree that reaches 15 to 30 feet, so a container is a compromise reserved for genetic-dwarf selections or space-limited gardens. It is workable but demands closer watering, feeding, and winter protection than an in-ground tree, and crops are lighter. Use the largest practical pot with excellent drainage, since the species will not tolerate a mix held wet against the roots.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: A potted persimmon dries far faster than one in the ground and has no deep soil to draw on, so check moisture daily in summer heat and water when the top inch or two is dry, until it runs from the drainage holes. Water more often than an in-ground tree, but never leave the pot standing in a full saucer, because continuously wet roots rot. Through dormancy the tree needs only enough to keep the root ball from drying out completely.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, so feed lightly and stop by late summer to avoid pushing tender growth into fall. Persimmon is a light feeder and excess nitrogen drops fruit, so keep container feeding conservative: a dilute balanced liquid feed a few times through the spring-to-midsummer flush is ample.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: A self-watering or sub-irrigated planter is not recommended for persimmon. Its reservoir keeps the lower root zone continuously moist, exactly the condition that triggers root and crown rot in this species. Persimmon needs a freely draining pot and a wet-then-dry cycle, not a constant water table against the roots.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: A self-watering pot (one with a water tank in the bottom) is a poor choice for persimmon. The tank keeps the lower roots wet all the time, and that constant wetness is just what rots persimmon roots. Use a pot that drains freely and let the soil dry a bit between waterings instead.
container_notes.container_overwintering_seasoned: Roots in a pot sit several zones colder than roots in the ground, so a persimmon hardy in your ground may still freeze its roots in a container. Before hard freezes, sink the pot to its rim in a bed or move it to an unheated but sheltered space (an attached garage or shed) that stays cold enough to hold dormancy while buffering the deep lows. The tree still needs its winter chill, so do not bring it into a heated room.
container_notes.container_overwintering_beginner: Roots in a pot get much colder than roots in the ground, so a persimmon that survives winter in your yard can still have its roots freeze in a pot. Before hard freezes come, either bury the pot up to its rim in a garden bed or move it to an unheated but protected spot like an attached garage or shed that stays cold but not deep-freezing. The tree still needs the cold to rest, so do not bring it into a warm room.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Annual crop rotation does not apply to persimmon: the tree holds its site for decades. Persimmon has no notable replant-disease reputation, unlike stone fruit, so the main site concern is simply drainage. Avoid planting where water stands or where a previous tree died of root or crown rot.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: You do not rotate a persimmon the way you rotate vegetables, because it stays in one place for many years. Persimmon does not have the replant problems that stone fruits do, so the main thing to avoid is a wet, poorly drained spot, or a place where another tree died of root rot.
rotation.good_after: any well-drained site in full sun with no standing-water history
rotation.note_seasoned: Choose the planting site for sun and drainage rather than for what grew before. Persimmon's one soil vulnerability is root and crown rot on wet ground, so a fresh, well-drained, full-sun position is what matters, not a rotation interval.
rotation.note_beginner: Pick the spot for sun and good drainage, not for what was there before. Persimmon's main weakness is root rot in wet soil, so a well-drained, sunny place is what counts.

growth_stages.name: Planting (bare-root or grafted, dormant)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late winter to early spring for bare-root; the cooler months for a grafted container tree, before bud break.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter or early spring for a bare-root tree, or the cooler months for a young potted tree, before the buds open.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A dormant tree with firm buds and healthy roots; on a grafted tree, the graft union (the swollen joint where the fruiting variety meets the rootstock) should sit above the final soil line.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A leafless young tree with firm buds and healthy roots. On a grafted tree, find the graft joint low on the trunk and keep it above the soil when you plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Handle the taproot gently (persimmon resents root disturbance), dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots, set the tree at nursery depth with the graft union above grade, backfill with native soil, and water in well. Do not fertilize in the hole. On heavy soil, plant on a raised mound.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Handle the roots gently, since persimmon does not like being disturbed. Dig a wide hole, set the tree at the depth it grew before with the graft joint above the soil, fill with the soil you dug out, and water well. No fertilizer in the hole. On heavy soil, plant on a mound.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the planting date, the cultivar, and whether it is Asian or American and its rootstock.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you planted, which variety it is, and whether it is an Asian or American persimmon.

growth_stages.name: Year-one establishment
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first full growing season after planting.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first whole growing season after you plant the tree.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Steady new shoot growth and a strengthening root system. Persimmon establishes slowly; do not expect fruit, and remove any that sets so energy goes to roots and framework.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Healthy new shoots and a tree settling in. Persimmon takes its time. Do not expect fruit yet, and pick off any that forms so the tree builds roots and branches.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply and regularly through the first season (persimmon's most water-sensitive period), keep a weed-free mulched circle around the trunk without piling mulch on the bark, and protect the trunk from string-trimmer wounds that invite borers.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Water deeply and often this first season, keep a mulched, weed-free circle around the trunk with the mulch off the bark, and keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk so borers have no wounds to enter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Log first-season watering and any early framework pruning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note your watering and any early shaping cuts.

growth_stages.name: Training (years one to three)
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: The first three years, the framework-building phase before reliable bearing.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: The first three years, while you build the tree's main branches and before it fruits much.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Persimmon is commonly trained to a modified central leader or open-center framework with well-spaced scaffolds. Its wood is somewhat brittle, so building a strong branch structure early pays off when heavy fruit loads arrive.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Persimmon is usually trained to a modified central-leader or open, vase-like shape with evenly spaced main branches. The wood is a bit brittle, so building strong branches early matters once the tree carries heavy fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly in dormancy to select well-spaced scaffolds and remove crossing or weak wood. Persimmon needs far less pruning than stone fruit; the goal is a sound framework and good light penetration, not heavy annual renewal.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Each winter, prune lightly to keep a few well-spaced main branches and remove ones that cross or are weak. Persimmon needs much less pruning than peaches; you are just building a strong, open shape.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record each dormant pruning and the scaffolds retained.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you prune each winter and which main branches you kept.

growth_stages.name: Winter dormancy
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Roughly December through February, the leafless months when the tree banks its (modest) chill.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: About December through February, the leafless winter months.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A leafless tree at rest, often still holding bright orange fruit that clings decoratively after the leaves drop. Persimmon needs only a modest amount of winter chill (roughly 100 to 200 hours for Asian types) to break dormancy evenly.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: A bare, resting tree, often still holding bright orange fruit after the leaves have fallen, which looks striking. Persimmon needs only a little winter cold (about 100 to 200 hours for Asian types) to wake up properly in spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little is required beyond winter sanitation: clear fallen and mummified fruit and prune out any dead or cankered wood while the structure is visible. Established trees need minimal water now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Not much to do beyond cleanup: clear fallen and dried-up fruit and cut out any dead branches while you can see the shape. An established tree needs very little water now.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note winter sanitation and any dormant pruning.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note any winter cleanup and pruning.

growth_stages.name: Dormant pruning
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late dormancy, roughly January into February, before growth resumes.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late winter, around January into February, before the tree wakes up.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches that show the framework clearly. Persimmon fruits on new growth from the previous season's wood, and its wood is brittle, so the aim is light structural pruning and thinning, not the hard renewal cuts stone fruit needs.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Bare branches, so you can see the whole shape. Persimmon fruits on new shoots and its wood breaks easily, so you only need light pruning to keep the shape and open the middle, not the hard cutting peaches get.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Prune lightly in late dormancy: remove dead, crossing, and weak wood, thin to let light in, and shorten overly long or heavy limbs to reduce breakage under a fruit load. Make clean cuts to limit the wounds that draw borers and canker.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Prune lightly in late winter: take out dead, crossing, and weak branches, thin to let light in, and shorten any long, heavy limbs so they do not snap under fruit. Make clean cuts so borers and disease have fewer wounds to enter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the dormant pruning date and roughly how much you removed.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note the day you pruned and how much you took off.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring, roughly May into June, notably later than most tree fruit, after the leaves are out.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring, around May into June, later than most fruit trees, after the leaves are already out.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small, inconspicuous cream-to-yellow flowers. Asian persimmons are self-fruitful and set fruit alone, often parthenocarpically (seedless); American persimmons are usually dioecious, so a female needs a male nearby unless it is a self-fruitful selection. Late bloom means frost is rarely a threat.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small, easy-to-miss cream or yellow flowers. Asian persimmons fruit on their own, often making seedless fruit with no pollen. American persimmons usually need a separate male tree nearby unless it is a self-fruitful kind. Because persimmon blooms late, frost is rarely a problem.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Little intervention is needed. Ensure a pollinizer is present for dioecious American females if fruit set is poor; otherwise let the self-fruitful tree set its own crop. Support bloom-time pollinator activity as a modest aid.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: There is little to do. If you have an American persimmon that is not fruiting, make sure a male tree is nearby. Otherwise let the self-fruitful tree set fruit on its own; bees visiting the flowers help a little.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record the bloom date and whether a pollinizer is present.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when bloom started and whether there is a male tree nearby (for American types).

growth_stages.name: Fruit set and drop
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Late spring into summer, after bloom, as young fruit forms and the tree sheds a portion of it.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Late spring into summer, after bloom, as small fruit forms and the tree drops some of it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit developing, followed by a natural early-summer drop of a share of it, which is normal. Excessive drop can signal water stress or over-fertilization (especially too much nitrogen). Persimmon rarely needs hand thinning.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Small green fruit forming, then a natural drop of some of it in early summer, which is normal. If a lot drops, the tree may be too dry or over-fed with nitrogen. Persimmon usually does not need you to thin the fruit by hand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep moisture steady to limit excess drop and hold off on heavy nitrogen. On a young tree carrying a heavy set on brittle wood, light thinning or limb support prevents breakage; otherwise let the tree self-regulate.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep the water steady to reduce fruit drop and do not over-feed with nitrogen. If a young tree is loaded and its branches might break, thin a little or prop the limbs; otherwise leave the tree to sort itself out.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Note the timing of the natural drop and any watering or feeding adjustments.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when the natural fruit drop happened and any changes to watering or feeding.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.timing_seasoned: Fall, roughly September through December depending on type and region; first meaningful crop around years three to five.
growth_stages.timing_beginner: Fall, usually sometime from September through December depending on the variety and where you live. The first real crop comes around years three to five.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Full orange color across the fruit. Non-astringent types (Fuyu) are picked firm and eaten crisp; astringent types (Hachiya, most American) are picked at full color and ripened to jelly-soft before eating. Fruit holds well on the tree and clips or twists free with the calyx attached.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The fruit turns fully orange. Firm types (Fuyu) are picked while still firm and eaten crisp; astringent types (Hachiya, most American) are picked when fully colored and then left to soften completely before eating. The fruit hangs on well and comes off with the leafy cap attached.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Clip or twist ripe fruit with the calyx intact rather than pulling, to avoid tearing. Harvest firm non-astringent fruit for crisp eating; pick astringent fruit at full color and counter-ripen. Fruit can be left hanging into cool fall weather, so harvest is unhurried.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Clip or gently twist off ripe fruit, keeping the leafy cap on, instead of yanking it. Pick firm types to eat crisp, and pick astringent types when fully orange, then let them soften on the counter. The fruit holds on the tree into cool weather, so there is no rush.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Record harvest dates, type (astringent vs non-astringent), and a rough yield.
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Note when you picked, whether it was a firm or soft type, and roughly how much you got.

notifications.title_beginner: Time to plant your persimmon tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Set a dormant bare-root persimmon now, or a grafted container tree in the cooler months, before growth resumes. Handle the taproot gently (persimmon resents disturbance), keep any graft union above the final soil line, choose a full-sun, well-drained spot, and plant on a raised mound if your soil is heavy. Do not fertilize in the hole.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is a good time to plant a bare-root persimmon, or a young potted tree in the cooler months, before it starts growing. Handle the roots gently, since persimmon does not like being disturbed, keep the graft joint above the soil, and pick a sunny, well-drained spot. On heavy soil, plant on a raised mound. Do not put fertilizer in the hole.

notifications.title_beginner: Time for a light winter prune
notifications.body_seasoned: Prune now, in late dormancy. Persimmon needs far less pruning than stone fruit: remove dead, crossing, and weak wood, thin for light, and shorten long or heavy limbs, since the wood is brittle and can break under a fruit load. Make clean cuts to limit borer and canker entry.
notifications.body_beginner: Prune now, in late winter, but go light. Persimmon needs much less cutting than peaches: take out dead, crossing, and weak branches, thin to let light in, and shorten any long, heavy limbs, since the wood breaks easily under fruit. Make clean cuts so borers and disease have fewer wounds to enter.

notifications.body_seasoned: Through its first two seasons a persimmon is most water-sensitive while roots establish. Water deeply and regularly at the root zone by drip or soaker, but let the soil dry between waterings, since persimmon is root-rot-prone and hates waterlogging. Keep a weed-free, mulched circle around the trunk and off the bark.
notifications.body_beginner: For its first couple of years, a young persimmon needs steady water while its roots get going. Give a deep soak at the ground every week or so, but let the soil dry a bit between waterings, since persimmon roots rot in soggy soil. Keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, with the mulch off the bark.

notifications.body_seasoned: Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so unlike early-blooming fruit it rarely loses a crop to frost. Asian persimmons are self-fruitful and set alone, often seedless; American persimmons usually need a male tree nearby unless yours is a self-fruitful selection like Meader. Little intervention is needed beyond confirming pollination for dioecious American females.
notifications.body_beginner: Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it usually does not lose its fruit to frost the way earlier trees do. Asian persimmons fruit on their own, often making seedless fruit. American persimmons usually need a separate male tree nearby, unless yours is a self-fruitful kind like Meader. There is little to do otherwise.

notifications.title_beginner: Some fruit will drop, and that is normal
notifications.body_seasoned: A share of the young fruit drops naturally in early summer, which is normal. Heavier-than-usual drop points to water stress or too much nitrogen, so keep moisture steady and go easy on feeding. On a young tree carrying a heavy set on brittle wood, thin lightly or support the limbs to prevent breakage.
notifications.body_beginner: Persimmon naturally drops some of its small fruit in early summer, so do not worry when it does. If a lot drops, the tree is probably too dry or was fed too much nitrogen, so keep the water steady and go light on fertilizer. If a young tree is loaded and branches might snap, thin a little or prop them up.

notifications.body_seasoned: Fruit is coloring up toward harvest. Pick non-astringent types (Fuyu) firm for crisp eating; pick astringent types (Hachiya, most American) at full orange color and ripen them to jelly-soft before eating, or they will pucker your mouth. Clip or twist fruit with the calyx attached. Persimmon holds on the tree into cool weather, so harvest is unhurried.
notifications.body_beginner: The fruit is turning orange. Pick firm types like Fuyu while still firm and eat them crisp. Pick astringent types like Hachiya when fully orange, then let them soften completely before eating, or they taste harshly puckery. Clip or twist the fruit off with the leafy cap on. The fruit hangs on into cool weather, so there is no rush.

notifications.body_seasoned: As the leaves fall, clear fallen and mummified fruit and rake up debris, which reduces overwintering anthracnose and other disease. Late summer through fall is also the time to check the trunk base for fresh gum and frass that signal borers, the one persimmon pest that can be serious.
notifications.body_beginner: As the leaves drop, clear away fallen and dried-up fruit and rake up the litter, which cuts down on disease next year. It is also a good time to check the bottom of the trunk for fresh ooze or sawdust, which can mean borers, the one persimmon pest that can be serious.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: In extreme heat, exposed persimmon bark and fruit can sunburn, showing as tan, sunken patches that later rot; this is why persimmon crops poorly in the hottest desert zones. Keep the tree well watered so heat and drought stress do not compound, and avoid stripping interior leaves that shade the fruit when you thin.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: In a strong heat wave, persimmon bark and fruit on the sunny side can sunburn, showing as tan, sunken spots that may rot; this is why persimmon does poorly in the hottest desert areas. Keep the tree watered so heat and dryness are not hitting it at once, and leave the leaves that shade the fruit.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry stretch, keep up deep watering
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Dry spell, do not let the tree run dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Deep, regular watering matters most in two windows: a young tree establishing its roots, and the fruit-development period, when erratic moisture drives fruit drop and small fruit. Soak deeply at the root zone and let the surface dry between waterings; an established persimmon tolerates moderate drought but sizes its crop poorly under sustained stress.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Deep, steady watering matters most for a young tree putting down roots and while the fruit is filling out, when uneven watering makes fruit drop. Give a deep soak at the ground and let the top dry out between waterings. An older persimmon takes some dryness, but the fruit stays small if it gets too dry.

weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Warm, humid weather favors anthracnose, which spots fruit and leaves in wet regions. Persimmon is otherwise a low-disease tree; keep the canopy open and dry, water only at the root zone, and remove any spotted or rotting fruit promptly so it does not seed more infection.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Warm, muggy weather can bring on anthracnose, which spots the fruit and leaves in rainy areas. Persimmon otherwise has few diseases. Keep the tree open, water only at the ground, and pick off any spotted or rotting fruit right away.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming, and that can help astringent fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Persimmon blooms late, so spring frost rarely threatens the crop. In fall, a light frost does not harm ripe fruit and in fact helps some astringent American persimmons soften and lose astringency. A hard freeze, however, can damage fruit still on the tree, so pick fully colored fruit ahead of a severe freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Persimmon blooms late, so spring frost rarely hurts the crop. In fall, a light frost does not harm ripe fruit and even helps some astringent American persimmons soften and lose their pucker. But a hard freeze can damage fruit still on the tree, so pick fully colored fruit before a severe freeze.

planting.text_seasoned: Handle the taproot gently and plant promptly: persimmon resents root disturbance, so a bare-root tree established quickly outperforms one left to dry or sit.
planting.text_beginner: Handle the roots gently and plant right away. Persimmon does not like having its roots disturbed, so getting it in the ground quickly helps it settle.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

planting.text_seasoned: Plant in full sun on a well-drained site or a raised mound; persimmon, especially Asian types, is prone to root and crown rot on wet ground.
planting.text_beginner: Plant where the tree gets full sun and the soil drains well, or on a raised mound. Persimmon roots rot in soggy soil, especially the Asian kinds.
planting.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: The first two seasons are the most water-sensitive; water deeply and regularly, but let the soil dry between soaks, since persimmon hates waterlogging.
establishment.text_beginner: Water deeply and often the first couple of years, but let the soil dry a bit between waterings. Persimmon needs steady water to establish but rots in soggy soil.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

establishment.text_seasoned: Keep mowers and string trimmers off the trunk base: the wounds they leave are the entry point for persimmon borer, the one pest that can kill a young tree.
establishment.text_beginner: Keep mowers and trimmers away from the bottom of the trunk. The wounds they leave let in borers, the one persimmon pest that can kill a young tree.
establishment.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

scaffold_formation.text_seasoned: Build a strong framework early: persimmon wood is brittle and heavy fruit loads can break poorly structured limbs, so favor well-spaced, wide-angled scaffolds.
scaffold_formation.text_beginner: Build strong branches early. Persimmon wood is a bit brittle and heavy fruit can snap weak limbs, so keep the main branches well spaced and spread out.
scaffold_formation.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Persimmon needs only modest winter chill (roughly 100 to 200 hours for Asian types), so it fruits across mild-winter zones where high-chill stone fruit fails.
dormancy.text_beginner: Persimmon needs only a little winter cold (about 100 to 200 hours for Asian types), so it fruits in mild-winter areas where peaches struggle.
dormancy.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormancy.text_seasoned: Clear fallen and mummified fruit over winter; it is the main overwintering source of anthracnose for the coming season.
dormancy.text_beginner: Clear away fallen and dried-up fruit during winter. It carries anthracnose disease into the next year.
dormancy.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Prune persimmon far more lightly than stone fruit: remove dead and crossing wood and thin for light, but avoid the hard renewal cuts peaches need.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Prune persimmon much more lightly than peaches: take out dead and crossing branches and thin to let light in, but skip the heavy cutting stone fruit gets.
dormant_prune.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Shorten long, heavy limbs to reduce breakage under fruit, and make clean cuts to limit the wounds that draw borers and canker.
dormant_prune.text_beginner: Shorten any long, heavy branches so they do not break under the fruit, and make clean cuts so borers and disease have fewer wounds to get in.
dormant_prune.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

blossom.text_seasoned: Persimmon blooms late (May to June), so it largely escapes the spring frosts that ruin earlier-blooming fruit, a major reliability advantage in frost-prone areas.
blossom.text_beginner: Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it usually dodges the spring frosts that wreck earlier fruit trees. That makes it more dependable in frosty areas.
blossom.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

blossom.text_seasoned: Know your type: Asian persimmons are self-fruitful and set alone (often seedless), while American persimmons are usually dioecious and a female needs a male nearby, unless it is a self-fruitful cultivar like Meader.
blossom.text_beginner: Know your type. Asian persimmons fruit on their own, often with no seeds. American persimmons usually need a separate male tree nearby, unless it is a self-fruitful kind like Meader.
blossom.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

fruit_set.text_seasoned: A natural early-summer fruit drop is normal; heavier drop usually means water stress or excess nitrogen, so keep moisture steady and feed lightly.
fruit_set.text_beginner: Persimmon naturally drops some small fruit in early summer, which is normal. Heavier drop usually means the tree is too dry or over-fed, so keep the water steady and go light on fertilizer.
fruit_set.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Match harvest to type: pick non-astringent Fuyu firm for crisp eating, and pick astringent Hachiya and American types at full color, then ripen to jelly-soft before eating.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick by type: harvest firm types like Fuyu while still firm and eat them crisp. Pick astringent types like Hachiya when fully orange, then let them soften all the way before eating.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

harvest.text_seasoned: Clip or twist fruit off with the calyx attached rather than pulling, and take advantage of persimmon holding well on the tree to harvest at leisure into cool fall weather.
harvest.text_beginner: Clip or gently twist the fruit off with the leafy cap on instead of yanking it. Persimmon holds on the tree well, so you can pick it over cool fall weeks without rushing.
harvest.author: claude_ai_gs_arc

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A mature standard persimmon commonly yields on the order of 100 to 300 pounds in a good year for a large American tree, and roughly 50 to 100 pounds or more for a well-grown Asian tree, depending on variety, age, and season. Persimmon tends to bear heavily and reliably once established, and rarely needs the thinning stone fruit demands.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: A grown persimmon can give a lot of fruit, often 50 to 100 pounds or more for an Asian tree and even more for a big American tree in a good year. Once it settles in, persimmon bears well and steadily, and you rarely need to thin the fruit the way you do with peaches.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Trees reach full bearing around years five to seven and stay productive for decades, with American persimmon especially long-lived. Asian persimmon in disease-prone humid regions may be shorter-lived where trunk canker is a factor.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: A persimmon hits full production around years five to seven and keeps bearing for decades. American persimmons are especially long-lived; Asian ones can be shorter-lived in humid areas where trunk disease is a problem.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Expect no crop in the planting year and little to none for the first two to three years. Remove any early fruit so the tree builds roots and framework; the first meaningful harvest typically comes around years three to five, with full bearing by years five to seven.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Do not expect fruit the first year, or really the first two or three. Pick off any early fruit so the young tree builds roots and branches. Your first real harvest usually comes around years three to five, with full crops by years five to seven.
factors_seasoned: adequate winter chill for the cultivar
summer heat and sunburn in desert zones
disease pressure (anthracnose, trunk canker) in humid regions

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No moon-phase planting preference is asserted. Extension sources do not support timing persimmon planting or care by lunar phase; site, drainage, chill matching, and type selection govern outcomes.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tree grows well but sets no fruit
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The tree is healthy but gives no fruit
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A vigorous tree that never fruits is most often an American persimmon female with no male pollinizer nearby, since American persimmons are typically dioecious. It can also simply be a young tree not yet of bearing age (three to five years), or occasionally an all-male seedling that will never fruit. The fix is type-aware: for a lone tree, choose a self-fruitful Asian variety (Fuyu, Hachiya) or a self-fruitful American selection (Meader); for existing American females, add a male American persimmon nearby.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: A healthy tree that never fruits is usually an American persimmon female with no male tree nearby, because American persimmons usually need separate male and female trees. It might also just be too young (persimmon takes three to five years), or a male seedling that will never fruit. The fix depends on the type: for a single tree, plant a self-fruitful Asian variety like Fuyu, or a self-fruitful American kind like Meader; if you have an American female, add a male American persimmon nearby.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Identify your tree's type and sex. Plant a self-fruitful Asian cultivar for guaranteed fruit on one tree, or ensure a male is present for a dioecious American female.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Find out what type and sex your tree is. A self-fruitful Asian variety fruits on its own; an American female needs a male tree nearby.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: The fruit is harshly astringent and puckers the mouth
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: The fruit is harshly puckery and dries out my mouth
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Intense astringency almost always means an astringent-type persimmon (Hachiya, most American types) was eaten before it was fully ripe. Astringent types are only edible once ripened to a jelly-soft, translucent stage, when the tannins have converted; picked or eaten firm, they are mouth-puckeringly tannic. This is not a defect but a type mismatch in handling. Non-astringent types (Fuyu) can be eaten firm and crisp with no such stage.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Harsh pucker almost always means you ate an astringent type (Hachiya, or most American persimmons) before it was fully ripe. Astringent kinds are only good once they turn completely soft and jelly-like; eaten firm, they are intensely puckery. It is not a bad fruit, just eaten too early. Firm types like Fuyu can be eaten crisp with no waiting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Ripen astringent types to full jelly-softness before eating (freezing or a warm spot speeds it), or plant a non-astringent Fuyu type you can eat firm.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Let astringent types get completely soft before eating (freezing them or a warm spot helps), or grow a non-astringent Fuyu type you can eat crisp.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Young fruit drops heavily before ripening
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Lots of small fruit falls off before it ripens
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Some early-summer fruit drop is a normal self-regulation, but heavy drop usually traces to water stress (erratic or insufficient moisture during fruit development) or over-fertilization, especially excess nitrogen, which persimmon responds to by shedding fruit rather than growing more. Young trees also naturally hold little fruit. The corrective action is steady moisture through fruit fill and a light hand with fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Persimmon naturally drops some small fruit in early summer, but heavy drop usually comes from uneven or too-little watering while the fruit is growing, or from too much fertilizer, especially nitrogen, which makes persimmon drop fruit instead of growing more. Young trees also just hold little fruit. The fix is steady watering while the fruit fills out and going light on fertilizer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture even through fruit development and avoid heavy nitrogen; on a young brittle-wooded tree, support or lightly thin a heavy set to prevent limb breakage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Keep the water steady while the fruit is growing and do not over-feed with nitrogen. On a young tree, prop up or lightly thin a heavy load so branches do not break.

succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Succession planting does not apply to persimmon. It is a permanent tree that occupies its site for decades and bears once each season as the fruit ripens in fall, so there is no staggered re-sowing to schedule the way there is for a short-season annual crop.
