3.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 3 winter lows (to about -40°F) exceed even American persimmon's roughly -25°F survival threshold, so the tree is likely killed. Not a persimmon zone.
3.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 3 is too cold even for American persimmon, which survives to about -25°F. This is not a persimmon-growing zone.

4.suitability_note_seasoned: The cold edge for reliable fruit. Only the hardiest American persimmons (Meader, Prok) survive zone 4's roughly -25°F, and the short season can leave late-ripening fruit unfinished. Asian persimmon will not survive here.
4.suitability_note_beginner: The cold edge. Only the hardiest American persimmons like Meader survive zone 4's deep cold, and the short season can leave late fruit unripe. Asian persimmon will not grow here.

5.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable American persimmon country. Cold-hardy cultivars (Meader, Prok, Yates) fruit dependably; the late bloom dodges spring frost and the season is long enough to ripen fall fruit. Asian persimmon is generally not hardy here.
5.suitability_note_beginner: Reliable American persimmon country. Hardy kinds like Meader and Prok fruit dependably, the late bloom dodges frost, and the season is long enough to ripen the fall crop. Asian persimmon usually will not survive.

6.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent American persimmon country across the full hardy cultivar range, with a comfortable season and abundant chill. Late bloom keeps frost a non-issue. The hardiest Asian cultivars on native rootstock are worth a try at the warm edge.
6.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent American persimmon country, with a comfortable season and plenty of winter cold. Late bloom keeps frost from being a problem. The very hardiest Asian kinds are worth a try in the milder parts.

7.suitability_note_seasoned: The transition zone where both types succeed: American persimmon thrives, and cold-hardy Asian cultivars (Fuyu, Great Wall, Saijo), especially on native rootstock, fruit reliably. A long fall carries late-ripening fruit to full color.
7.suitability_note_beginner: The overlap zone where both types work: American persimmon thrives, and cold-hardy Asian kinds like Fuyu and Great Wall fruit reliably, especially on native roots. A long fall ripens even late fruit.

northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: Up north, grow American persimmon, which is very cold-hardy. It fruits well from zone 5 to 7, is marginal in zone 4, and too cold in zone 3. Asian persimmon usually will not survive here except the hardiest kinds in zone 7. Persimmon blooms late, so the limit is deep winter cold, not spring frost.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: The northern tier is American persimmon (D. virginiana) country: it is very cold-hardy, fruiting reliably from zone 5 through 7, marginal in zone 4, and too cold in zone 3. Asian persimmon is generally not hardy here except the hardiest cultivars on native rootstock in zone 7. Late bloom means spring frost is rarely the limit; midwinter cold is.
northern_tier.chill_basis_seasoned: Northern-tier winters bank far more chill than any persimmon needs, so chill is never the limiter here; cold-hardiness is. American persimmon survives roughly -20 to -25°F and covers this whole region except the very coldest zone 3.
northern_tier.chill_basis_beginner: Winters here are plenty cold for persimmon's low chill needs. The challenge is not too little cold but too much: only the very cold-hardy American persimmon survives, and even it is pushed in zone 3.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Reliable, classic persimmon country for both types. Ample chill, a long warm season, and the full Asian and American cultivar range. Watch anthracnose and trunk canker in wet years and favor native rootstock on heavier soils.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Reliable, classic persimmon country for both types. Plenty of winter cold, a long warm season, and any variety works. Keep an eye on wet-weather disease and use trees on native roots for heavier soil.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon (Fuyu, Hachiya) reliably given persimmon's low chill need, with an early, long harvest. American persimmon also fruits well. Disease and drainage are the variables, not chill.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon like Fuyu and Hachiya reliably, since persimmon needs little cold, with a long harvest. American persimmon does well too. The things to watch are disease and drainage, not cold.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon (Fuyu, Hachiya) reliably given persimmon's low chill need, with an early, long harvest. American persimmon also fruits well. Disease and drainage are the variables, not chill.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon like Fuyu and Hachiya reliably, since persimmon needs little cold, with a long harvest. American persimmon does well too. The things to watch are disease and drainage, not cold.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: Great persimmon country. Both American and Asian persimmon grow well in zones 8 and 9, and the firm-eating Asian Fuyu is a Southern favorite. In this humid climate keep an eye on leaf and fruit disease, and use trees grafted on native roots for heavier soil.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: Classic persimmon country. Both American and Asian persimmon thrive across zones 8 and 9; the non-astringent Asian Fuyu is a Southeastern favorite. Anthracnose and trunk canker are the main disease considerations in the humid climate, and native rootstock helps on heavier soils.
se_gulf.chill_basis_seasoned: Southeastern winters bank roughly 350 to 1,000 chill hours, far more than persimmon's modest need, so chill is never limiting. Both types crop dependably; the variables are humidity-driven disease and soil drainage.
se_gulf.chill_basis_beginner: Winters across the Southeast easily meet persimmon's low chill needs, so any type fruits. The things to watch are wet-weather disease and heavy soils, not cold.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Prime Asian persimmon country with ample chill and long sunny falls; the full cultivar range fruits reliably, Fuyu and Hachiya especially. Frost is a non-issue given late bloom.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Prime Asian persimmon country, with plenty of winter cold and long sunny falls. Any variety fruits reliably, especially Fuyu and Hachiya. Frost is not a problem because persimmon blooms late.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: The lower valley fruits Asian persimmon reliably with an early bloom and a long harvest from fall into early winter. Chill is ample for the full cultivar range.
9.suitability_note_beginner: The lower valley fruits Asian persimmon reliably, with an early bloom and a long harvest into early winter. There is plenty of winter cold for any variety.

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: Excellent Asian persimmon country. Interior California, the Central Valley, grows Fuyu and Hachiya beautifully in zones 8 and 9, with plenty of winter cold and long, sunny falls. Persimmon blooms late, so frost is seldom a problem.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: Prime Asian persimmon country. Interior California (the Central Valley) grows commercial Fuyu and Hachiya across zones 8 and 9 with excellent fruit quality, ample chill, and long, sunny falls. Frost is rarely an issue given persimmon's late bloom.
ca_interior.chill_basis_seasoned: Interior California banks roughly 300 to 1,100 chill hours, well above persimmon's modest need, so chill is never the limit. Both astringent and non-astringent Asian persimmon fruit reliably.
ca_interior.chill_basis_beginner: The Central Valley gets plenty of winter cold for persimmon, so any variety fruits. It is one of the best places in the country to grow Asian persimmon.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Mild maritime zone 9 fruits Asian persimmon reliably; persimmon's low chill need is easily met and the climate avoids both hard freeze and extreme heat.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Mild coastal zone 9 fruits Asian persimmon reliably. Persimmon needs little winter cold, which the coast gives, and it avoids both hard freezes and extreme heat.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: Warm coastal zone 10 still banks enough chill for low-chill Asian persimmon, which fruits reliably with a long, late harvest into early winter. A dependable, ornamental dooryard tree.
10.suitability_note_beginner: Warm coastal zone 10 still gets enough winter cold for low-chill Asian persimmon, which fruits reliably with a long, late harvest into early winter. A dependable, good-looking backyard tree.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: The mild coast suits Asian persimmon well in zones 9 and 10. Persimmon needs little winter cold, which the coast provides, and it avoids both hard freezes and extreme heat. A reliable, good-looking backyard tree here.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Mild maritime conditions suit Asian persimmon well across zones 9 and 10. Persimmon's low chill requirement is easily met, and the mild coast avoids both hard freeze and extreme heat. A dependable, attractive dooryard fruit here.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: North-coast California banks roughly 150 to 800 chill hours, comfortably above persimmon's low requirement, so even the mild coast delivers enough to fruit Asian persimmon reliably.
ca_north_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The North Coast has mild winters, but persimmon needs so little cold that it fruits fine here, unlike high-chill fruit that struggles on the coast.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Slightly inland zone 9 banks enough chill (about 200 to 550 hours) for Asian persimmon to fruit reliably. A common, productive dooryard tree; frost and heat are non-issues.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Slightly inland zone 9 gets enough winter cold for Asian persimmon to fruit reliably. It is a common, productive backyard tree here, with no frost or heat trouble.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest coastal zone 10 banks low chill (about 50 to 350 hours), so low-chill Asian cultivars (Fuyu, Izu) fruit but marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the variable.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The warmest coast gets little winter cold, so low-chill Asian kinds like Fuyu and Izu fruit but only marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the uncertain part.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest coastal ground banks low chill (about 50 to 350 hours), so low-chill Asian cultivars (Fuyu, Izu) fruit but marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the variable.
11.suitability_note_beginner: The warmest coast gets little winter cold, so low-chill Asian kinds like Fuyu and Izu fruit but only marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the uncertain part.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: Asian persimmon is a common backyard tree along the Southern California coast. Slightly inland zone 9 fruits reliably; the warmest coastal zone 10 gets little winter cold and fruits marginally, better in cooler years. Frost and heat are not problems here; winter chill is the only question.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: Asian persimmon is a common, productive dooryard tree across the Southern California coast. Inland zone 9 sites fruit reliably; the warmest coastal zone 10 sites bank low chill and fruit marginally, better in cooler years. Heat and frost are non-issues; chill adequacy is the only variable.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_seasoned: South-coast California banks roughly 50 to 550 chill hours. Inland zone 9 (about 200 to 550 hours) comfortably meets persimmon's low need; the warmest coastal zone 10 (about 50 to 350 hours) is marginal in warm winters but still fruits low-chill Asian cultivars.
ca_south_coast.chill_basis_beginner: The Southern California coast is mild, but persimmon needs so little cold that inland areas fruit reliably and even the warmest coast fruits in cooler years, unlike high-chill fruit that fails here.

9.suitability_note_seasoned: Desert zone 9 banks just enough chill for low-chill Asian persimmon, but extreme summer heat sunburns bark and fruit, so it is marginal. Choose a low-chill cultivar, water generously, and keep canopy shading the fruit.
9.suitability_note_beginner: Desert zone 9 gets just enough winter cold for low-chill Asian persimmon, but fierce summer heat sunburns the fruit and bark, so it is only marginal. Pick a low-chill variety, water well, and keep leaves shading the fruit.

10.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest desert zone 10 barely meets low-chill needs and pushes fruit into brutal summer heat and sunburn; only the lowest-chill, earliest cultivars are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.
10.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert zone 10 barely gets enough winter cold and bakes the fruit in extreme summer heat and sunburn. Only the lowest-chill, earliest kinds are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.

11.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest desert barely meets low-chill needs and pushes fruit into brutal summer heat and sunburn; only the lowest-chill, earliest cultivars are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.
11.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert barely gets enough winter cold and bakes the fruit in extreme summer heat and sunburn. Only the lowest-chill, earliest kinds are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: You can grow Asian persimmon in the California desert, but it is marginal. There is just enough winter cold, and the bigger problem is fierce summer heat that sunburns the bark and fruit. Pick a low-chill Asian variety, water well, and keep leaves shading the fruit. Crops are lighter than in cooler areas.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: Asian persimmon can be grown in the California desert but is marginal: winter chill is just met, and the real limit is extreme summer heat, which sunburns bark and fruit. Choose a low-chill Asian cultivar, water generously, and shade or leave canopy over exposed fruit. Crops are lighter and less certain than in cooler regions.
ca_desert.chill_basis_seasoned: Low-desert California banks roughly 100 to 400 chill hours, just meeting persimmon's low need. Chill is barely adequate; the binding constraint here is summer heat and sunburn, not chill or cold, so these zones are marginal rather than reliable.
ca_desert.chill_basis_beginner: The desert gets just enough winter cold for low-chill Asian persimmon, but the real trouble is extreme summer heat that sunburns the fruit and bark. That is why persimmon is only marginal here.

8.suitability_note_seasoned: Established persimmon country. Both native American persimmon and widely adapted Oriental persimmon fruit reliably with ample chill and a long season; low-maintenance and pest-tolerant. Plant on well-drained soil (Asian persimmon is root-rot-prone) and favor native rootstock.
8.suitability_note_beginner: Good persimmon country. Both native American persimmon and adaptable Asian persimmon fruit reliably, with plenty of winter cold and a long season, and little pest trouble. Just plant in well-drained soil, since Asian persimmon roots rot in wet ground; native rootstock helps.

warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: Good persimmon country. Across the warm, dry interior like the Texas hill country, both American persimmon (which is native there) and Asian persimmon grow well and need little spraying or pruning. Just plant in well-drained soil, since Asian persimmon roots rot in wet ground; native rootstock helps.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: Established persimmon country. Across the warm-arid interior (the Texas hill country and similar), both American persimmon (native here) and Oriental persimmon are widely adapted and dependable, needing little spraying or pruning. Well-drained soil matters, since Asian persimmon is root-rot-prone; native rootstock helps.
warm_arid.chill_basis_seasoned: Warm-arid interior winters bank roughly 450 to 850 chill hours, comfortably above persimmon's modest need, so chill is not the limit. Both types fruit reliably; the main site concern is drainage.

description_seasoned: Persimmon (Diospyros) is a handsome, low-maintenance deciduous fruit tree that yields some of the easiest home fruit there is, plus fiery orange-to-scarlet fall color and bright fruit that clings decoratively after the leaves drop. It comes in two very different forms. The Asian or Oriental persimmon (D. kaki) is the dooryard favorite: self-fruitful, low-chill, hardy to about USDA zone 7, with large fruit in non-astringent types eaten crisp like an apple (Fuyu) or astringent types ripened to a sweet, jelly-soft pulp (Hachiya). The American persimmon (D. virginiana) is far more cold-hardy, to roughly zone 4, but is usually dioecious, so a female needs a male tree nearby unless you plant a self-fruitful selection like Meader. Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it largely dodges the spring frosts that plague earlier fruit, and it is famously untroubled by pests and diseases. It asks little: full sun, well-drained soil, light pruning, and patience for the first three to five years.
description_beginner: A persimmon is a good-looking fruit tree that drops its leaves each winter and gives you one of the easiest crops you can grow, with brilliant fall color and bright orange fruit that hangs on after the leaves fall. There are two main kinds. The Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) is the popular one for backyards: it fruits on its own, needs little winter cold, and handles down to about zone 7, with firm types eaten crisp like an apple (Fuyu) and soft types ripened until sweet and jelly-like (Hachiya). The American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is much hardier, down to about zone 4, but usually needs separate male and female trees, unless you plant a self-fruitful kind like Meader. Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it usually escapes the spring frosts that hurt earlier fruit trees, and it hardly ever has pest or disease trouble. It just needs full sun, well-drained soil, a little pruning, and a few years of patience.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Persimmon is ready when the fruit reaches full, deep orange color. For non-astringent types (Fuyu), that plus a firm feel means ready to pick and eat crisp. For astringent types (Hachiya and most American persimmons), full color means ready to harvest, but not yet to eat: they must then ripen to a jelly-soft, nearly translucent stage before the astringency clears. Clip or twist fruit free with the calyx (the leafy cap) attached rather than pulling. The fruit holds on the tree well into cool fall weather, so harvest can be unhurried.
harvest_ready_beginner: A persimmon is ready when the fruit turns fully deep orange. For firm types like Fuyu, orange plus a firm feel means you can pick and eat it crisp. For astringent types like Hachiya and most American persimmons, orange means ready to pick but not yet to eat: let them sit until completely soft and jelly-like, when the pucker is gone. Clip or gently twist the fruit off with the leafy cap on instead of pulling. The fruit hangs on well into cool fall weather, so you do not have to rush.
bloom_time_seasoned: Persimmon blooms in late spring, typically May into June, after the leaves have expanded and notably later than most tree fruit. The flowers are small and inconspicuous, cream to yellow. This late bloom is a major advantage: it means persimmon rarely loses a crop to the spring frosts that threaten earlier-blooming apple, peach, and plum.
bloom_time_beginner: Persimmon flowers in late spring, usually May into June, after the leaves are already out and later than most fruit trees. The flowers are small and easy to miss, cream or yellow. Blooming late is a big plus, because it means persimmon almost never loses its fruit to the spring frosts that hurt earlier trees like peaches and apples.
hardiness_notes_seasoned: Persimmon hardiness depends entirely on type. American persimmon (D. virginiana) is very cold-hardy, surviving roughly -20 to -25°F, and fruits reliably across zones 5 to 9 (marginal in zone 4, too cold in zone 3). Asian persimmon (D. kaki) is more tender, injured or killed below about 10°F, and is best in zones 7 to 10, with some cold-hardy Asian cultivars (Great Wall, Sheng) extending its range a little on native rootstock. Taken together the species spans zones 4 to 10: American covers the cold end, Asian the warm. The warm limit is set less by heat than by insufficient winter chill and, in the hottest deserts, by fruit and bark sunburn.
hardiness_notes_beginner: How cold a persimmon can take depends on which kind it is. American persimmon is very hardy, surviving about -20 to -25°F, and fruits well from zone 5 to 9 (marginal in zone 4, too cold in zone 3). Asian persimmon is more tender and can be killed below about 10°F, so it does best in zones 7 to 10, with a few cold-hardy Asian kinds reaching a bit colder. Between the two, persimmon covers zones 4 to 10: pick American for cold areas and Asian for milder ones. In the hottest deserts, the limits are too little winter cold and sunburn on the fruit and bark.
chill_hours_note_seasoned: Persimmon has a low chilling requirement, which is a big reason it succeeds across mild-winter regions where high-chill stone fruit fails. Asian persimmon needs only about 100 to 200 hours below 45°F, and some cultivars less; American persimmon needs somewhat more but is still modest. This low chill, combined with late bloom, makes persimmon one of the most broadly adaptable temperate-to-subtropical fruits. Only the near-chill-free deep tropics (south Florida, lowland Hawaii) fall short for standard cultivars.
chill_hours_note_beginner: Persimmon needs only a little winter cold (called chill hours) to bloom properly, which is why it grows in mild-winter places where peaches struggle. Asian persimmon needs only about 100 to 200 hours of cold below 45°F, and some kinds less. That low need, plus its late bloom, makes persimmon one of the most adaptable fruit trees. Only the warmest, nearly frost-free tropics (south Florida, lowland Hawaii) are too warm for the usual varieties to fruit.
pollinator_notes_seasoned: Pollination is the headline difference between the two persimmon types, and it decides whether you need one tree or two. Asian persimmon (D. kaki), including non-astringent Fuyu and astringent Hachiya, is self-fruitful: a single tree sets a full crop alone, and its main cultivars are parthenocarpic, forming seedless fruit with no pollen at all. American persimmon (D. virginiana) is the opposite: it is typically dioecious, carrying male and female flowers on separate trees, so a female needs a male American persimmon within roughly 50 to 200 feet to fruit. The exceptions are self-fruitful American cultivars such as Meader, bred to set seedless fruit with no male present. The two species do not cross-pollinate each other, and even among self-fruitful types, planting a pollinizer often gives heavier, seedier crops. For most home gardeners the simple path is one self-fruitful Asian tree; choose the American route (a hardy female plus a male, or a self-fruitful selection like Meader) where winters are too cold for Asian persimmon.

For most gardeners the easy choice is one self-fruitful Asian tree; go with American (a female plus a male, or a self-fruitful kind like Meader) where winters are too cold for the Asian type.

establishment_note: Most persimmons begin bearing about 3 to 5 years after planting.
recommended_rootstock_note: Asian persimmon is commonly grafted onto native D. virginiana for cold and wet-soil tolerance; choose rootstock for your soil and climate, not for tree size.

rootstock_options.name: Diospyros virginiana (American persimmon)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for your Asian variety grafted on native D. virginiana for cold-hardiness and wet-soil tolerance.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: The standard rootstock for Asian persimmon in the Southeast and cold regions. Native D. virginiana is very cold-hardy and more tolerant of heavy, wet soils and root rot than kaki on its own roots, and it improves anchorage. The trade-off is a tendency to sucker. The default choice where drainage is marginal or winters are cold.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: The usual rootstock for Asian persimmon in the South and in cold areas. Native persimmon roots are very cold-hardy and handle heavy, wet soil and root rot better than the Asian type on its own roots. The downside is that it tends to send up suckers. A good default where soil is heavy or winters are cold.

rootstock_options.name: Diospyros lotus (date-plum)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for D. lotus rootstock for vigorous, well-drained sites; it is less tolerant of wet soils than native persimmon.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: A vigorous rootstock used for Asian persimmon, valued for uniformity and a fibrous, easily transplanted root system. It is less tolerant of heavy, wet soils than native D. virginiana and somewhat less cold-hardy, so it suits well-drained sites in milder regions.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: A vigorous rootstock for Asian persimmon that transplants easily and grows uniformly. It does not handle wet, heavy soil as well as native persimmon and is a bit less cold-hardy, so it fits well-drained ground in milder areas.

rootstock_options.name: Diospyros kaki (seedling)
rootstock_options.what_to_ask_nursery: Ask for kaki seedling rootstock only for warm, well-drained sites; it is the least tolerant of wet soil and cold.
rootstock_options.traits_seasoned: Asian persimmon on its own (kaki seedling) rootstock is used in warm, well-drained climates such as California, giving good vigor and graft compatibility. It is the least tolerant of wet soils (most root-rot-prone) and the least cold-hardy of the common rootstocks, so it is reserved for favorable sites.
rootstock_options.traits_beginner: Asian persimmon grown on its own seedling roots, used in warm, well-drained places like California. It grows well there but is the most prone to root rot in wet soil and the least cold-hardy, so it is only for good sites.

year_one_notes_seasoned: In the planting year, prioritize establishment over fruit. Plant a dormant bare-root or grafted tree, handle the taproot gently, keep a weed-free mulched circle around the trunk, and water consistently through the first two seasons while letting the soil dry between waterings. Remove any fruit that sets. Hold off on fertilizer at planting and keep any feeding light, since persimmon is a light feeder and excess nitrogen only drops fruit. Protect the trunk base from mower and trimmer wounds that invite borers.
year_one_notes_beginner: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a bare-root or young grafted tree, handle the roots gently, keep a mulched, weed-free ring around the trunk, and water it steadily through the first couple of seasons while letting the soil dry a bit between waterings. Pull off any fruit that forms. Do not fertilize at planting, and keep any feeding light, since too much, especially nitrogen, just makes fruit drop. Keep mowers and trimmers away from the trunk so borers cannot get in.
first_harvest_notes_beginner: Persimmon takes its time, usually giving a first crop somewhere in the third to fifth year. The most important thing to sort out is which type you have, because it changes how you harvest completely. A non-astringent type such as Fuyu is picked firm and eaten crisp, like an apple. An astringent type such as Hachiya, and most American persimmons, is picked at full orange color but is not edible yet: it has to sit until it goes completely soft and jelly-like before the pucker clears. Either way, clip or gently twist the fruit off with its leafy cap attached rather than pulling. A natural fruit drop in early summer is normal; a heavy one usually means water stress or too much nitrogen.
first_harvest_notes_seasoned: First cropping typically falls between years three and five. Cultivar type governs harvest protocol entirely and is the fact to establish first: non-astringent types (Fuyu) are picked firm and eaten crisp, while astringent types (Hachiya and most American persimmons) are harvested at full color but require post-harvest ripening to a jelly-soft, nearly translucent stage before astringency clears. Detach by clipping or twisting with the calyx attached rather than pulling. Early-summer physiological drop is normal; disproportionate drop indicates water stress or excess nitrogen. Build the framework deliberately while the tree is young, because persimmon wood is brittle and heavy fruit loads break poorly structured limbs, so well-spaced, wide-angled scaffolds are worth more here than on a tougher-wooded species.
full_harvest_notes_beginner: From about the fifth year the tree carries a full crop, and it is an unusually relaxed harvest. Persimmon blooms late, in May or June, so it escapes the spring frosts that ruin earlier fruit, and the fruit then hangs on the tree well into cool fall weather, so there is no rush to strip it. Harvest by type: pick Fuyu and other non-astringent kinds firm for crisp eating, and pick Hachiya and American types at full deep orange, then let them ripen indoors until they are jelly-soft before you eat them. Clip or twist each fruit off with its leafy cap on. Prune far more lightly than you would a peach, and shorten any long, heavy limbs so they do not break under a load of fruit.
full_harvest_notes_seasoned: Full production from roughly year five. Two characteristics make this the least time- pressured harvest on the roster: late bloom in May to June, which largely evades the spring frost events that cost earlier-blooming fruit their crop, and prolonged on-tree holding into cool fall weather. Harvest remains type-scoped: non-astringent cultivars firm for crisp consumption, astringent cultivars at full color followed by ripening to jelly-soft before eating. Detach with the calyx attached. Dormant pruning is far lighter than stone fruit, limited to dead and crossing wood and thinning for light, with no hard renewal cuts; shorten long, heavy limbs specifically to reduce breakage, since persimmon wood is brittle, and make clean cuts to limit the wounds that admit borers and canker.
